Name: tracing_edit_transfer
Title: Does Tracing Tell You Where to Edit? Testing the Locus-Edit Link Across Models
Short Hypothesis: The layers/components flagged by causal tracing as decisive for a fact do not reliably predict the best editing location, and this tracing-editing dissociation-documented for single models-holds systematically across model families and relations; a better predictor of edit success is a direct edit-efficacy probe rather than tracing peaks. Localization for reading differs from localization for writing.
Related Work: Hase et al. (2023) show causal tracing does not predict editability within a model. We test the generality of this dissociation across models, relations, and editing methods, and propose and evaluate an alternative edit-location selector-turning a single-model observation into a systematic cross-model account and a practical method.
Abstract: Causal tracing identifies where a fact is causally read, and model-editing methods often target those layers. But reading and writing localization may differ. Building on evidence that tracing does not predict editability, we test the generality and offer a remedy. Across multiple model families, relations, and editing methods, we compare edit success when targeting tracing-peak layers versus other layers, and we develop a direct edit-efficacy predictor: a cheap forward-backward probe estimating each layer's leverage on the output for the specific fact. We hypothesize (i) tracing peaks systematically fail to coincide with best-edit layers across models; (ii) the dissociation's size varies by relation and method in predictable ways; and (iii) the edit-efficacy predictor selects better edit locations than tracing, improving edit success and specificity. We evaluate with standard editing benchmarks, reporting edit success and ripple/specificity by target-selection strategy. Establishing a systematic tracing-editing gap and a better selector would correct a common methodological assumption, explain inconsistent editing results, and provide a practical, tracing-free method for choosing where to edit-improving the reliability of knowledge updates across models.
Experiments: 1. Across several models, run causal tracing to get peak layers per fact. 2. Perform edits at tracing-peak vs swept alternative layers; measure edit success and specificity. 3. Build an edit-efficacy predictor (per-layer output leverage via gradients); compare its chosen layers to tracing. 4. Evaluate success/specificity by selection strategy across relations and methods. Metrics: tracing-peak vs best-layer overlap, edit success/specificity by target, predictor vs tracing performance, cross-model consistency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Editing benchmarks and methods are heterogeneous, complicating comparison. The edit-efficacy predictor may itself be method-specific. Best-edit layer is defined by chosen metrics. Results may vary with model scale and architecture.
